Measurement Parameter Estimates with Standard Errors

Source: R/measurement_se.R
measurement_estimates.Rd

Returns the measurement parameters of a fit_mixture() fit – the item probabilities, the class means and variances, the count rates – and the class-size logits, each with a standard error, a z statistic and a two-sided p-value. It is the standard-error companion to measurement_summary(), which prints the same estimates without them.

Usage

measurement_estimates(fit, se = c("robust", "hessian", "opg"))

Arguments

fit

A model returned by fit_mixture().

se

Which standard-error estimator: "robust" (default), "hessian" or "opg". See Details.

Value

A data frame with one row per parameter and class: block (the sub-model for a mixed or blocked measurement model, NA otherwise), parameter ("probability", "mean", "variance", "rate" or "class_logit"), item, category (polytomous items only), class, estimate, se, z, p_value and boundary. The covariance matrix of the reported parameters is attached as the attribute "vcov".

Details

The standard errors come from the log-likelihood of the fitted model, differentiated with respect to the parameters on the scale the fit estimates them on (logits for probabilities, logs for rates and standard deviations, means as they are) and carried to the reported scale by the delta method. The three estimators are those of growth_estimates():

  • "robust" (the default) is the sandwich \(H^{-1} B H^{-1}\) (White, 1982), which stays valid when the within-class model is only approximately right – for instance, normal indicators whose real within-class distribution is skewed, or variances held equal across classes when they are not.

  • "hessian" is the inverse observed information, the textbook maximum-likelihood variance when the model is correct.

  • "opg" is the inverse outer product of the case scores.

A gap between "robust" and "hessian" is a sign of misspecification. Sample weights and a cluster variable are honoured as in growth_estimates().

A parameter held equal across classes – a variance under variances_equal = TRUE – is repeated once per class, with the same standard error, as in measurement_summary().

The estimates maximise the log-likelihood plus the prior that keeps them off the edge of the parameter space (bayes_constants in fit_mixture()), so the information is that sum's: the prior's curvature is added to \(H\), and to \(B\) as well, so that "robust" reduces to "hessian" when the model holds. In \(B\) the prior's curvature is taken on each parameter's natural scale (logits, log rates, and for a variance the precision \(1/\sigma^2\), on which the variance prior's curvature does not depend on the data). With bayes_constants = 0 these are the textbook likelihood estimators. With covariates on class membership fitted in one step, the class probabilities belong to the covariate model and no class-size logits are reported (see coef()); under n_steps = 3 the standard errors are those of the step-1 model, which is where the measurement parameters are estimated.

Probabilities at the boundary

An item probability that has run to 0 or 1 (within 0.001) is flagged in the boundary column, and a message says how many there are. Its standard error is not interpretable: the likelihood is flat in that direction, so any number would measure how far the optimiser stopped from the edge rather than how precisely the data pin the probability down. A probability whose logit has run past \(\pm 15\) is therefore held where it stopped, as a fixed value, and its standard error is NA; the other parameters' standard errors are those of the model with it fixed.

References

White, H. (1982). Maximum likelihood estimation of misspecified models. Econometrica, 50(1), 1-25. doi:10.2307/1912526

Louis, T. A. (1982). Finding the observed information matrix when using the EM algorithm. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 44(2), 226-233. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1982.tb01203.x

See also

measurement_summary(), growth_estimates() for growth models, and plot.mixture_model(), whose error_bars draw these standard errors on the profile bar chart.

Examples

set.seed(1)
X <- rbind(matrix(rnorm(300, 0), 100), matrix(rnorm(300, 2), 100))
fit <- fit_mixture(X, n_classes = 2, measurement = "continuous",
                   n_init = 5)
measurement_estimates(fit)
